words.intro: Every two years every German car goes to the TÜV, where a calm person in overalls looks underneath it, and either gives it a coloured sticker or ends your summer.

grammar[0].fact: German has an extraordinary *Handwerker* system. A plumber or electrician has passed long exams, and a *Meister* can train others. To get one in a city you may have to wait for weeks. People with a good one don’t tell their friends.

grammar[1].fact: German signs say *Betreten verboten* or *Auf eigene Gefahr*, at your own risk. And the sign *Eltern haften für ihre Kinder*, parents are liable for their children, hangs on building sites everywhere, though it means much less in law than it seems to.

document.intro: Two real plates on an old machine for a laundry. The black one tells you who built it. The red one is the *Technischer Überwachungs-Verein* in Vienna, an early TÜV, saying someone has checked it.
document.fact: Those letters still mean what they did: Technischer Überwachungsverein, technical inspection association. And an old car that still passes is said, with some pride, to have *noch zwei Jahre TÜV*.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Say what you had done, with lassen in the Perfekt.
document.tasks[1].items[2].answer: Ich habe das Öl wechseln lassen.
reading.intro: Max’s car, formerly Anna’s, formerly Tom’s, is due at the TÜV. Max knows nothing about cars, so he has let Lena’s uncle look at it, and now it’s his turn with the inspector, Frau Kolb. She has been lying under cars for twenty-six years, and she has seen everything. Until today.
reading.photos[0].caption: Hier wird dein Auto geprüft. An der Wand sieht es lustiger aus, als es ist.
reading.fact: The *TÜV* began in the 1860s as a steam-boiler inspection service, after boilers kept exploding. Today it also tests cars, lifts and fairground rides. The sticker on your number plate shows, by colour, the year your car is next due.
